sections.h2: What is it like to sell a house in Warminster, PA?
sections.html:
Warminster is a Bucks County township of 10 square miles and an estimated 33,254 residents, and a sale there starts with the township's Licenses and Inspections Department, which expects a permit application for any property being sold. Applications go in online, and the department answers questions at 215-443-5423. After that, the sale follows Pennsylvania's normal disclosure, recording and tax steps.

The township has been on the map since 1711, when its borders were set, and it started as farmland under early English and Scotch-Irish settlers. Almost all of its housing came later. As recently as 1955 it had no residential subdivisions and one housing complex, and then the population jumped from 7,127 in 1950 to 34,900 in 1970. Most houses you will see on a listing sheet come from that postwar build-out.

sections.h2: Why did Warminster grow so fast, and what does that mean for sellers?
sections.html:
The Navy's presence at the Johnsville site drove the township's mid-century growth, and that shapes today's housing stock. The U.S. Navy took over an industrial site from Brewster Aeronautical Corporation in 1943, and the Naval Air Warfare Center there operated until 1996. The same site later trained astronauts for the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo programs. Today the township's larger employers include ABB, Burpee Seeds, CRC Industries, Havis and a Penn State research laboratory.

One local issue deserves a straight answer in any sale. Several of the township's groundwater wells have been contaminated with PFOS and PFOA from the former Navy site, the Navy paid for treatment systems, and the Warminster Municipal Authority now buys more water from the North Wales Water Authority. The authority supplies water and sewer to about 10,300 customers. If your house is on public water, buyers may ask about it, so keep a recent water bill and the authority's contact details ready.

  • Neighbors include Warrington, Warwick, Ivyland, Northampton, Upper Southampton, Hatboro and Horsham.
  • Villages inside the township include Davisville, Hartsville, Johnsville, Rosewood Park and Warminster Heights.
  • The township maintains 13 parks covering 420 acres, led by the 243-acre Warminster Community Park.

sections.h2: How do I get the township permit needed to sell in Warminster?
sections.html:
You apply through the township's online portal, and the Licenses and Inspections Department handles the review. Its page says plainly that making changes, renting a property or selling a property each need a permit, and that applications are submitted online. Staff can tell you which permit fits your situation if you call before applying.

Take these steps in order:

  • Call 215-443-5423 or email the department before you list so you know the permit name and fee for a residential sale.
  • Submit the application online and pay the fee through the portal.
  • Ask whether an inspection is part of the process, schedule it if so, and fix anything it flags.
  • Give your agent or settlement attorney a copy of the approved permit for the closing file.

Start the application early. If repairs are needed, time them against your settlement date, since a closing date in the agreement of sale does not move on its own.

sections.h2: Which schools and transit serve Warminster?
sections.html:
Warminster is part of the Centennial School District. The township's public schools are Davis, McDonald and Willow Dale elementary schools, Log College Middle School and William Tennent High School. Archbishop Wood Catholic High School and Nativity of Our Lord School are the parochial options inside the township.

For commuters, SEPTA's Warminster station is the terminus of the Warminster Line into Center City Philadelphia, and City Bus Route 22 runs south from the township through Willow Grove to North Philadelphia. The DART East bus runs weekdays along PA 132. Major roads include PA 132 (Street Road), PA 263 (York Road) and PA 332 (Jacksonville Road), and the township maintains 100.83 of its 113.97 miles of public roads. PECO supplies electricity and gas, and trash service runs under a township contract.

sections.h2: What do I owe at closing and how do Bucks County rules apply?
sections.html:
Bucks County's recorder says the realty transfer tax is 2 percent, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district, paid when the deed is recorded. It is a tax on the value conveyed, which is not always the sale price, and the sale agreement usually divides it between buyer and seller. Since January 2026 the recorder no longer takes personal checks for the tax: cash in the office, cashier's check, money order or credit card only.

Family transfers can be exempt, but you must still present the state's Statement of Value (REV-183) where the exemption is not stated in the deed. Your attorney or title agent handles that paperwork. The seller must also deliver the property disclosure statement under 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303 before the agreement is signed, and Act 74 of 2026 adds a flood-insurance notice that sellers provide once the Insurance Department posts its flood information.

On the assessment side, the Bucks Board of Assessment Appeals set August 3, 2026 as the 2026 annual appeal deadline, which has passed, and annual appeal changes take effect the following tax year. The homestead and farmstead filing deadline is March 1 for the tax year starting July 1. Buyers must send contact information to the Board within 30 days of purchase under Act 29, so tell your buyer.

sections.h2: Should I list or sell as-is in Warminster?
sections.html:
Listing suits a house in good condition on a street with recent sales, and an as-is cash sale suits a house that needs work or a seller on a short clock. Cash buyers usually offer less than a repaired, listed house would bring, in exchange for speed and fewer contingencies. Ask any buyer who takes the house as-is how the township permit will be handled.

  • Ask for a written offer with a closing date and proof of funds.
  • Find out whether the buyer will accept a house that has not yet received the township permit and who handles it.
  • Compare the offer against a net sheet for a listing sale, including permit costs and repairs.

faqs.q: Does Warminster require a permit to sell a house?
faqs.a: Yes. The Licenses and Inspections Department says selling a property needs a permit, and applications are made online. Call 215-443-5423 before applying to confirm the permit type and fee.

faqs.q: What is a typical home value in Warminster?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau reports a median owner-occupied home value of $418,600 for 2020 to 2024. Your price depends on condition and nearby sales, so the median is only a reference point.

faqs.q: Should I mention the PFOS and PFOA wells to Warminster buyers?
faqs.a: Be ready to discuss it. The Warminster Municipal Authority has closed wells with PFOS and PFOA contamination from the former Navy site, installed treatment systems paid for by the Navy, and buys more water from a neighboring authority. Direct buyers to the authority for current water quality reports.

faqs.q: Where do I record the deed for a Warminster house?
faqs.a: At the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds, usually through your title company or attorney. The recorder collects the 2 percent transfer tax at recording and no longer accepts personal checks for it.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Warminster house that I inherited?
faqs.a: Yes, once the person with authority over the estate signs. Pennsylvania's disclosure chapter exempts transfers by an estate fiduciary, though many sellers still give buyers a condition statement. Ask the estate's attorney who may sign.
